lead: A hypervisor, also called a virtual machine monitor, is the software layer that creates and runs virtual machines on one physical host. It exists to share CPU, memory and devices among isolated guests while keeping each guest inside its own virtual hardware. Cloud providers use it to sell small VMs from large servers; a laptop user runs it to test another operating system. Examples include Xen, ESXi and Hyper-V on servers, and VirtualBox and Workstation on desktops. This chapter explains the two placements, the control domain, CPU rings, vCPU scheduling and device emulation.
prereq: You need: 3.2, which places the hypervisor among implementation levels.

blocks.text: A hypervisor is software that creates and runs virtual machines. The same idea has another name: virtual machine monitor, or VMM. It sits between the physical hardware and the guest operating systems. It gives each guest a virtual CPU, virtual memory and virtual devices. It also keeps guests apart: one guest cannot read another guest's memory through normal instructions.

Why does it exist? A physical server is often too large for one small job. The hypervisor turns one server into many smaller machines. A cloud provider can then rent a 2 vCPU VM to one customer and a 16 vCPU VM to another. On a laptop, a developer can run Linux inside Windows without rebooting.

There are two standard placements. A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware; it is also called bare-metal. Xen, VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V are Type 1. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host operating system; it is also called hosted. Oracle VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are Type 2. The figure shows both. The difference matters: Type 1 has no general-purpose host OS between it and the hardware, so it controls devices and scheduling directly. Type 2 borrows the host OS for drivers and file systems, which is convenient on a laptop but adds a layer of delay.

sections.h3: Control domain, rings and vCPU scheduling

blocks.text: In Xen, the first VM, called domain 0 or Dom0, is privileged. It runs a driver VM that talks to real devices and offers services to other guests. Other guests are unprivileged domains, sometimes called domU. The hypervisor is still the lowest layer; Dom0 is a helper, not the hypervisor itself. Hyper-V uses a parent partition in a similar role. Some designs call this a service VM or control domain.

x86 processors have privilege rings 0 to 3. Ring 0 is most privileged; ring 3 is least. In a plain OS, the kernel runs in ring 0 and applications in ring 3. A hypervisor needs ring 0 for itself. A guest kernel cannot run in ring 0, or it could control the machine. Hardware-assisted virtualization solves this with two modes: a root mode for the hypervisor and a non-root mode for guests. The guest kernel still believes it is in ring 0, but the CPU exits to the hypervisor on sensitive instructions. Older or para-virtual designs put the guest kernel in ring 1 and trap sensitive calls; see 3.4.

Each guest sees one or more virtual CPUs, or vCPUs. The hypervisor's scheduler maps runnable vCPUs onto physical CPU cores. It gives each vCPU a time slice, saves its registers, and switches to another vCPU. If a host has 8 cores and the guests have 12 vCPUs in total, the hypervisor can overcommit: at most 8 vCPUs run at one instant. Overcommit raises utilisation but makes latency less predictable. Details of CPU virtualisation are in 3.5.

A guest cannot touch a real disk or network card directly unless the hypervisor allows it. Device emulation is the default: when the guest writes to a virtual device register, the hypervisor traps the access, performs the operation on a real device, and returns the result. This works with unmodified guests and lets many VMs share one card. The cost is CPU time per I/O operation. A second option is passthrough: the hypervisor gives one VM direct control of a device, often through an IOMMU, a unit that translates device addresses. Passthrough is fast but the device is no longer shared. A third option is a split driver: a front-end driver in the guest talks to a back-end driver in the control domain; Xen uses this model. The choice affects throughput, isolation and how many VMs can use the device. For the storage and network layers above this mechanism, see 3.6.

figure.caption: Following the 16 GB laptop down the chain: after the host OS takes 4 GB and the Type 2 hypervisor takes 1 GB, only 11 GB is free, so the 12 GB virtual machine falls 1 GB short and cannot start at that size without overcommit or ballooning.

spec.title: RAM budget of the worked example
spec.aria: A downward chain of six boxes starting from total physical RAM of 16 GB, subtracting 4 GB for the host OS and 1 GB for the Type 2 hypervisor to leave 11 GB free, then showing the virtual machine asks for 12 GB and is short by 1 GB.

examples.question: A laptop has 16 GB of RAM. The host OS uses 4 GB and a Type 2 hypervisor uses 1 GB. A virtual machine is configured with 12 GB of guest RAM. (a) Find the free RAM before the VM starts. (b) Find the shortfall if the VM tries to use its full 12 GB. (c) Can the VM get all 12 GB without overcommit or ballooning?
steps: RAM left after the host OS = 16 − 4 = 12 GB.
RAM left after the hypervisor = 12 − 1 = 11 GB. This is the free RAM before the VM starts.
The VM asks for 12 GB. Shortfall = 12 − 11 = 1 GB.
Without overcommit or ballooning, the hypervisor cannot promise the missing 1 GB, so the VM cannot get its full 12 GB.
examples.answer: Free RAM before the VM is 11 GB; the VM is short by 1 GB, so it cannot get its full 12 GB without overcommit or ballooning.
examples.check:
total = 16.0
host = 4.0
hypervisor = 1.0
vm = 12.0
free_before = total - host - hypervisor
shortfall = vm - free_before
print(f"{free_before:.1f}")
print(f"{shortfall:.1f}")

traps: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware; a Type 2 hypervisor needs a host OS underneath. Do not draw Type 2 as bare-metal.
The hypervisor is not the guest operating system. Each VM carries its own guest OS image and its own kernel.
A control domain such as Xen Dom0 is a privileged VM that helps with I/O and management; it is not the hypervisor itself.
A vCPU is a virtual CPU, not a physical core. More vCPUs than cores is overcommit; it does not create extra hardware.
Device emulation costs CPU time per I/O. Passthrough is faster but takes the device away from other VMs.

quiz.q: Define a hypervisor and give its other common name.
quiz.a: A hypervisor is software that creates and runs virtual machines on a physical host. Its other name is virtual machine monitor, or VMM.

quiz.q: Name two Type 1 hypervisors and two Type 2 hypervisors.
quiz.a: Type 1: Xen, VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V. Type 2: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

quiz.q: Why does a Type 2 hypervisor need a host operating system, and what cost does that add?
quiz.a: The Type 2 VMM runs as an application on the host OS and uses the host's drivers and file systems. The extra layer adds delay and dependence on the host OS.

quiz.q: What is a privileged control domain? Use Xen Dom0 as the example.
quiz.a: It is a privileged VM that helps the hypervisor manage real devices and guest services. In Xen, Dom0 runs driver code and control tools; other guests are unprivileged domains.

quiz.q: A host has 32 GB RAM. The host OS uses 6 GB and the hypervisor uses 2 GB. A VM is configured with 20 GB. Find the free RAM before the VM and the spare or shortfall.
quiz.a: Free = 32 − 6 − 2 = 24 GB. The VM needs 20 GB, so spare = 24 − 20 = 4 GB. There is no shortfall.

quiz.q: A guest kernel executes a privileged instruction under hardware-assisted virtualization. Describe what the hypervisor and CPU do.
quiz.a: The guest runs in non-root mode. The sensitive instruction causes a CPU exit to the hypervisor in root mode. The hypervisor emulates or validates the operation, then resumes the guest with the result.

quiz.q: Why can vCPU overcommit improve utilisation but hurt predictability?
quiz.a: Overcommit lets more vCPUs exist than physical cores, so idle guest time can be filled and utilisation rises. When many vCPUs become runnable together, each waits for a core, so response time and latency vary more.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CPUs add hardware-assisted virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) and IOMMU features such as Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi. SR-IOV lets one physical network card present many virtual functions to VMs with near-native speed. Confidential computing extends the hypervisor model with encrypted guest memory, so the host cannot read it; AMD SEV and Intel TDX are examples. MicroVMs such as Firecracker shrink the device model for faster startup in serverless platforms. Search for hardware-assisted virtualization, SR-IOV, confidential VMs and microVM.
